title: Homogeneous functions and first-order homogeneous equations
section: Homogeneous Equations ▷ Scaling and the substitution y=xv
terms: homogeneous function; homogeneous degree; homogeneous first-order equation; substitu- tion y=xv; scale invariance; Euler identity for homogeneous functions.

exposition.text:
n
A function H is homogeneous of degree n if H(tx, ty) = t H(x, y) whenever the scaling and
expressions are defined. A first-order equation M dx + N dy = 0 is called homogeneous in this
sense when M and N have the same degree. Where division is valid, its slope depends only on
the ratio y/x.
′ ′ ′ ′
Set y = xv, so y = v + xv , to reduce y = F(y/x) to xv = F(v) − v, a separable equation.
Ratios v with F (v) = v give straight-line solutions and can disappear if one divides by F (v) − v.
The substitution works on intervals avoiding x = 0. This meaning of homogeneous is distinct
from a linear equation having zero forcing term.
n
For differentiable H homogeneous of degree n, differentiating H(tx, ty) = t H(x, y) with respect
to t at t = 1 gives Euler's identity xH + yH = nH. This is the identity used to recover one

Set v = y/x. Then v + xv = v + v , so dv/v = dx/x. Integration gives −1/v = log x + C.
At x = 1, v = 1, so C = −1 and y = x/(1 − log x). Its maximal positive interval containing 1

question.text:
A differentiable function F (x, y) is homogeneous of degree 3. If F(1, 2) = 5 and F (1, 2) = 1,
x
what is F (1, 2)?
y
(A) 5 (B) 2 (C) 7 (D) 14 (E) 15

solution.text:
Euler’s identity is xF + yF = 3F . At (1, 2) this gives 1 + 2F = 15, so F = 7.
